summary_html: A child dies or suffers serious harm while **under agency supervision**, constituting systemic failure. Federal law mandates disclosure and review to identify causes and reforms.
authority_html:
- **Protect Our Kids Act (PL 112-275)** — federal commission and review requirements  
- **CAPTA §5106a(b)(2)(A)(x)** — mandates public disclosure of child-fatality cases

case_law.method: v1.1.0 case-law rebuild: authorities selected per decision point, each opinion retrieved from CourtListener and read; holding and quote taken from the opinion text; independently re-verified before release. Previous keyword-matched Justia listings were removed.

key_cases.case_name: DeShaney v. Winnebago County Department of Social Services
key_cases.court: Supreme Court of the United States
key_cases.holding: The Due Process Clause imposes no general affirmative duty on a child-protection agency to protect a child from private violence, even where the agency knew of the danger and failed to act.
key_cases.relevance: Marks the constitutional boundary at this node: outside state custody there is no affirmative federal duty to protect, so a failure here is answerable through state law, licensing and federal funding conditions rather than § 1983 — which is why the Texas remedy has been systemic litigation (M.D. v. Abbott) rather than individual damages.
key_cases.quote: a State's failure to protect an individual against private violence simply does not constitute a violation of the Due Process Clause

key_cases.case_name: M.D. ex rel. Stukenberg v. Abbott
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Texas long-term foster children have a substantive due process right to be free from an unreasonable risk of harm, and the State's caseworker-caseload and monitoring failures supported class-wide liability, although the district court's injunction was significantly overbroad.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling systemic authority for Texas: it is the Fifth Circuit's framework for caseworker caseloads, placement oversight and monitoring of children in DFPS conservatorship, and — because Suter forecloses private Title IV-E enforcement — it is the mechanism that has actually produced federal oversight of this node in Texas.
key_cases.quote: we hold that the General Class and the LFC subclass were properly certified

key_cases.holding: Texas does not recognize a negligence per se claim for failing to report child abuse under Family Code § 261.109; the reporting duty is enforced criminally, not through private tort liability.
key_cases.relevance: The controlling Texas answer to the question families ask at this node: the § 261.101 duty to report and the § 261.109 misdemeanor for failing to report create no private cause of action, so a failure to report (or to act on a report) is punished criminally and administratively, not in a civil damages suit.
key_cases.quote: we hold that it is not appropriate to adopt Family Code section 261.109(a) as establishing a duty and standard of conduct in tort

key_cases.case_name: Doe v. Taylor Independent School District
key_cases.court: United States Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit
key_cases.holding: Schoolchildren have a Fourteenth Amendment liberty interest in bodily integrity that a teacher's sexual abuse violates, and school officials may be personally liable under § 1983 for supervisory failures that manifest deliberate indifference to that right; the principal's claim survived summary judgment while the superintendent received qualified immunity.
key_cases.relevance: The en banc standard for holding a supervisor responsible when a child in an institution's care is seriously harmed — deliberate indifference, not negligence, and not respondeat superior.
key_cases.quote: In short, supervisory liability for deliberate indifference to constitutional violations committed by subordinates was clearly established when the events in this case occurred.
